items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续Alison Cotton一贯模糊的跨界风格，将民谣、前卫音乐与宗教氛围融为一体。中提琴、簧风琴、击弦古钢琴与钢琴构成核心编制，本作新增鼓、贝斯与合成器，扩展了声音层次。多数曲目为即兴创作，一次性录制完成，营造出近乎神秘的静谧感。《I Am!》以John Clare的诗作为词，搭载持续嗡鸣的低音之上；《Sprigs of Heather》开篇呼应中世纪圣咏，随后转为钢琴主导的缓慢级进旋律，结构精炼。专辑同时也是Cotton对2024年末去世父亲的纪念，《The Final Harvest》描绘父亲最后一次造访他所钟爱的小菜园，情感含蓄而深沉。光与暗在不同曲目间流转渗透，情绪不断位移，整体超越了任何单一风格标签的界定。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦Analog Africa厂牌发行的贝宁传奇乐队Orchestre Poly-Rythmo与歌手Antoine Dougbé合作时期的合集，涵盖1977至1982年间的作品。Dougbé以腿部击拍演绎Cavacha节奏著称，与乐队共同呈现融合伏都教传统、古巴son与刚果伦巴的西非放克。乐评特别分析《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》中合成器铺垫与高帽主导的律动，以及《We Tayi Sin Assi Tche》中明显的古巴影响，包括牛铃与鼻音应答唱法。录音年代赋予声音塑料质感的吉他音色与合成器介入，区别于此前的合辑。对于挖掘非洲放克、传统仪式音乐如何转化为流行形式的听众，这张合集提供了少见的历史维度，展现了贝宁音乐在七十年代与加勒比及周边非洲流派深度互动的面貌。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由一位瑞典提琴手、两位挪威乐手合作，以两国传统舞曲为素材，却刻意摆脱舞场功能与常规民乐语汇。三件乐器在私密而即兴的室内乐对话中不断拆分旋律、节奏与织体，竖笛、萨克斯、风袋及鼓组也模糊了传统与现代的边界。评论尤其指出作品会突然停滞、碎裂，显露舞曲欢快表面下的幽暗与不安，因此其价值主要在于对民间音乐的再诠释和跨文化实验，而非提供纯粹的传统演奏。

items.body: It is Monday morning, checkout time at Grand Hotel Viljandi, and a German festival goer with his wristband still on hands back his room card and asks what a double costs. Not for tonight, he specifies, for the same weekend next July, when Viljandi Folk comes round again, and preferably the very same room he has just spent four nights in. The receptionist explains that the system will not take a booking more than 11 months out. He takes this badly. He has plainly been turning it over for a while, perhaps since Thursday’s wild folk dances, perhaps during the downpour on Sunday night just before the grand finale, and now there is nothing to be done with the thought except carry it home.  That is a fairly standard state to leave Viljandi in. The town has something to do with it. Seventeen thousand people live on a ridge above a long glacial lake in southern Estonia, forest running down to the water on the far shore and the ruins of a 13th-century Livonian Order castle at the centre, the ground falling away in wide grass terraces cut by deep ravines. Those terraces are the festival: four outdoor stages sitting in the folds of the hills, Kaevumägi (Well Hill) at the top, the two Cherry Hills (Kirsimägi I & II) below it, and the Song Festival Grounds down on the flat. Two indoor rooms handle the rest: the Traditional Music Centre beside the ruins, the Ait or granary as locals call it, and the Sakala Centre in town, carrying the quieter programme by day and the wilder dances by night. Everything is ten minutes’ walk from everything else. To cross between Kaevumägi and the ruins you take the suspension bridge, 50 metres of it slung over a 13-metre trench and still swaying under everyone who steps on. Black sheep graze the slopes throughout, unbothered by any of it. And the festival is not only up on the ticketed grounds. It spills straight down into the old town, where two free stages run from lunchtime to eleven at night across all four days: the Green Stage on Laidoneri Square, where the dance schools set out workshops so anyone can learn the steps, and Sõprade Hoov on Lossi Street, a village-party yard open to any musician who fancies a turn. Seventy concerts happen out here, matching the paying stages exactly, strung along a street lined with a craft and design market where nobody checks a wristband. The programmed players are only half of it. Buskers of every age sprout across town, under gazebos and on pavements, some barely tall enough to hold the instrument, playing to whoever slows down. What carries across those slopes, alleyways and squares is pärimusmuusika, a word the English ‘folk’ flattens badly. For four days in late July this town does not commemorate its traditions so much as live inside them and shove them somewhere new. Most of what you hear sits on archival foundations: village fiddle tunes, bagpipe repertoire, regilaul runic song, the older Estonian and Finno-Ugric layers that were collected, catalogued and came within a generation of vanishing. Yet none of it is handled as museum material. This year’s theme, ‘To Each Their Own Instrument,’ was taken literally. Stages were packed with uncommon, traditional instruments most people couldn’t name, and within a day half of them were queuing to try one. Inside the Ait, the festival kept a second timetable. On three of the four nights, Thursday, Friday and Saturday, its great hall turned into Tantsumaja, the dance house, running from around 11pm until three or four in the morning while a rotating cast of folk musicians kept the tunes coming in relay. What happened on the floor was not a taught routine so much as a shared fluency: circles and couples moved through the room side by side, skill levels visibly ranging from a first attempt to real virtuosity, yet the general standard stayed remarkably high, dancers who had grown up on this repertoire picking out the shape of a tune they had never heard before and finding the steps inside it before the first verse was out. It all began, as it always does, with the parade winding through town on the Thursday early afternoon, before mayor Jaak Pihlak handed the ceremonial key to festival chief Ando Kiviberg, who has run this since its first edition in 1993. Just over 7,000 people came through the gates across that afternoon and evening, more day-one pass buyers than last year. In the Ait, six students turned the theme into a play, To Each Their Own Instrument, staged by director Lee Taul with a cast drawn from the Viljandi Culture Academy, the Estonian Academy of Music and Theatre and Tartu’s Eller college. Bagpipe, kannel and Teppo-type accordion were carried through the story by players still young enough to be studying them, the archive walking and talking rather than sitting in a case. The same idea took physical form a few streets over, on Pikk Street beside St John’s Church, where Pilliküla opened to the public for the first time: an ‘instrument village’ of close to 80 free workshops where anyone could sit down with a teacher and coax a first note out of a kannel, a bagpipe, a jaw harp, a fiddle, a talharpa or an accordion. “Musical heritage lives on as long as playing an instrument is common enough among the people,” Kiviberg said of the idea behind Pilliküla, the point being that a tradition survives by being played, not preserved. You could see the results all over town that weekend. Children busked on the hills and street corners with whatever they could play, one girl of maybe twelve and her violin set up between two stages with her case open for coins, taking more by evening than some of the market stalls. Up on the stages, the theme got loud. On II Kirsimägi that first afternoon, Gangar dug century-old dance tunes out of Norway’s national archives and ran them through a rock band. The Oslo five-piece build off springar and gangar rhythms, the old triple-time and walking dances they take their name from, Hardanger fiddle ringing over a rhythm section that a rhythm section hammering underneath, and drive the lot flat out. They played here in 2022, so they knew the crowd would dance, and it did. Down on the Song Festival Grounds, the sounds pulled from much further away. The Zawose Queens held the first Tanzanian booking in Viljandi’s history, and the sky opened just as they were due on, the kind of delay that empties a field. It did not. People pulled up hoods and waited, and by the time Pendo Zawose and her niece Leah came on, the wait had sharpened the air: Wagogo polyphony over ilimba thumb pianos and chizeze fiddle, a London rhythm section laying psychedelic rock beneath, a rain-soaked crowd that had chosen to be there. Their grandfather Hukwe Zawose carried this music around the world but never once let the women of his family sing lead; two generations on, his daughter and granddaughter stood at the front of the stage. The rain never really let up on the first evening, and neither did the appetite for dancing in it. Manhu closed Kaevumägi from half nine, five Sani players from the farming villages of the Stone Forest of Yunnan, together since 2003. They build from the lusheng, a bamboo mouth-organ whose drone sets the whole thing running, then stack the three-string adiza and call-and-response singing on top, with bass and drum kit worked so far underneath that the village music always keeps the upper hand. This is the sound of Sani daily life, drinking songs, welcome songs, love songs, seasonal tunes, nearly all of it built to move to, and they run a set the same way: a tune, a stop to walk the crowd through the steps, then the tune again, faster. Not a full sentence of English passed between the five of them and none was needed. One lifted a single leaf to his lips and bent a melody out of it; the steps were called by demonstration, arms up, follow this. By the last stretch a cold, soaked Estonian crowd that had never heard Sani music in its life was strung across the grass doing Yunnan courtship dances in the rain. Outdoors, the weather could be worn like a badge. Indoors, it exposed the festival’s one real weakness. Early shows had already packed the Ait to the walls. Over at the Sakala Centre, TõnisMägi, whose “Koit” became an anthem of the 1988 Singing Revolution, sold out fast enough to leave a queue stranded at a closed door, though these days the noise around him owes as much to his divisive public stances as to his songs. It happened repeatedly over the next three days: too many people, too few seats, and indoor rooms never built for crowds this size. Friday opened, in the early afternoon, on Ruhnu, with music and tales that had come closer than most to disappearing for good. Sounds and Stories from Ruhnu Island takes its name from a speck in the Gulf of Riga, Runö in Swedish, that held a few hundred ethnic Swedes and their own fiddle tradition until 1944, when the Soviet advance emptied the island almost overnight and left the repertoire alive only on tape. Fiddlers Karoliina Kreintaal and Lee Taul, with storyteller Kairi Leivo, have spent years playing it back off those recordings, and here they did it as a one-off. Ruhnu-born storyteller Jüri Keskpaik told the island’s life from the inside, its weddings, feasts, church and sea, while three members of the Nordic supergroup Groupa sat in: fiddler Mats Edén, flautist Jonas Simonson, and Terje Isungset, the Norwegian percussionist who builds his instruments from wood, stone and ice, all three back on Kaevumägi a few hours later for Groupa‘s own set. Behind them the whole time ran the island itself, archive film of Ruhnu’s shoreline, its people, customs and dances, a vanished community moving on screen while its own tunes played live underneath. Later that afternoon Mari Kalkun, born and raised in the Võru country of Estonia’s south-east and one of the few keeping its endangered Võro language sung, brought her kannel up against the kokle of Latvian player Laima Jansone. The kannel and the kokle are cousins, box zithers grown from the same ancient Baltic instrument and drifted so far apart that their traditions barely recognise one another now. Set them back together and that separation is nowhere to be heard: Kalkun’s playing drifting and psychedelic, her voice carrying the Võro songs she has spent a career prising out of the archive, against Jansone’s harder, more rhythmic attack, the two instruments circling, answering, now and then locking into a single line as though they had never parted. Then Kalkun left the stage entirely, microphone in hand, and walked into the middle of the field to sing from there, the crowd falling quiet and closing around her as she moved. In the evening, Amaro Duho kept their tradition in the family, literally. Matild Dobi assembled the band in 2021 from her own children, four decades after she helped start Ando Drom, one of the great names in Hungarian Roma music, and the point was to hold the songs together rather than let them scatter. It showed. Oláh Roma tradition on guitar, tambura and accordion, their own tunes threaded through the inherited ones, all of it played with the loose, unforced ease of people who do this around a table at home and happened, that night, to be doing it in front of a few thousand strangers. Estonian tradition can be handled far less gently, and Mandoterror proved it: a distorted rhythm section and a mandolin screaming where a lead guitar should be, five players who take Estonian folk melody and hit it at Nordic-metal weight. Kristjan Kuusmik stood out front on vocals, Tanel Sakrits‘ mandolin carrying the tunes a fiddle would usually hold, the old material cranked through songs from last year’s Nõiajaht and the anthem ‘Oru Leeni’. There is no compromise in it. The melodies land as though they were originally written for the extra volume: fast, sharp, and carrying clean across the grounds. The bigger stages found their real heat once it got dark, starting with Zetod on the Song Festival Grounds, the set that, by the reckoning of more or less everyone there, was where the festival properly began. Formed in Värska in 2003, they take Seto leelo, the old polyphonic singing of Estonia’s south-eastern border country, and play it at the speed and volume of a punk band: short hard songs stacked back to back, every word in Seto dialect, the pit moving from the first number and a whole field firing the lines back. In keeping with the year’s theme they built the set around four fiddles, one apiece, over accordion, bass and drums, the old dance tunes and archive material driven hard and fast. The singing that once went slow and unaccompanied, one voice leading and the rest answering, comes out here distorted and double-time, and nobody down the front drops a syllable. Most of the pull is frontman Jalmar Vabarna, who has fronted the band since they were teenagers and, off the stage, happens to be the elected ülemsootska, earthly stand-in for the Seto king. Same job either way, really, carrying his own corner of the country in front of as many people as will have it. By Saturday the site was full, 11,000 through the gates and the biggest crowd of the four days, the paths between stages packed from early afternoon as people wove from one set to the next. It all spilled onto the Song Festival Grounds, where HrayBery had the whole arena linking hands. The Polish-Ukrainian band rebuild village dance music from old scores and field recordings of the San river valley, a border region of eastern Galicia once shared by Poles, Ukrainians, Jews and Roma before post-war deportations scattered its people. They looked the part, in the Sunday best of a century ago: straw boater hats over dark suits and waistcoats for the men, high-collared white blouses and pale skirts for the women. Two fiddles, hammered dulcimer and frame drum drove the kolomyjkas, mazurkas, polkas and kozaks, and the crowd read the cue: great circling chains across the concrete, ring inside ring, while the grass banks behind filled with people watching them turn. A couple of hours later, still on the Grounds, the picture shrank from a full folk band to two women over a single instrument. Duo Ruut are Ann-Lisett Rebane and Katariina Kivi, who sit facing each other across one kannel, close enough to touch, one plucking while the other bows or drums the body, their voices soaring into harmonies that can hold a field still. Here they broke that on purpose, billing the set as Duo Ruut³ and pulling in Indrek Mällo on bass, Jaan Jaago on electric guitar, and on percussion Tõnu Tubli, who drummed a decade in Trad.Attack! and had already remixed the duo’s tunes on his own record. Outdoors, the expanded setup carried and got people moving, but it cost something too: the fine, quiet tension of two players negotiating one instrument is what makes them extraordinary, and a rhythm section inevitably paints over it. Still, once a real beat was locked under the runo song, the Grounds went from hushed to dancing. Over on II Kirsimägi, the boundary between the stage and the dirt dissolved entirely. Orkesta Mendoza opened with ‘Cumbia Volcadora’, six of them in matching suits, though nothing stayed buttoned down for long. Sergio Mendoza ran the set from the keys with an accordion slung across his chest, and on his shout of “¡Derecha! ¡Izquierda!” the whole field threw its hands right, then left, in time with him. Quetzal Guerrero sawed at the violin like an acrobat, Ozzy Acosta’s percussion kept the cumbia turning underneath, and Victor Hugo drove the band from the kit. Mendoza grew up in Ambos Nogales, the town the US-Mexico border splits in two, and the Orkesta plays what that town might sound like with the line gone: mambo, cumbia and ranchera rammed into surf guitar, psychedelia and indie rock. The Grounds kept filling as night came on, until the weekend’s largest crowd, some 8,000—packed in for Puuluup. Ramo Teder and Marko Veisson play the talharpa, a bowed lyre all but extinct outside the island of Vormsi, except they drum, bow, pluck, and brush it, feeding horsehair through loopers until a knocking, creaking rhythm rises out of a single ancient instrument. For a few numbers they brought out company: Tubli was back behind a kit, slamming real drums into a stage the pair usually run on loops and horsehair alone. In tuxedos and flat deadpan, Veisson’s voice rumbling low beneath Teder’s higher line, they sang in Estonian and a language of their own invention, stopping dead between numbers to sell the crowd straight-faced nonsense about what they’d just played. It was Veisson’s 50th, and when the field found out, thousands sang him happy birthday. He answered the only way that suited the night: throwing himself off the front to crowd-surf the field. They tried out new dance routines on the spot, saving their wildest choreography for a set that felt looser and warmer than usual. By the end, Duo Ruut were up there too: Rebane and Kivi crowding the microphones alongside Teder, Veisson, and Tubli, all five packed around the stand to see it out. Puuluup had warmed the field. OOPUS came to pound it. Mari Meentalo fed bagpipe, jaw harp and regilaul into a looper and handed the loops to Johannes Ahun’s analogue Roland synths, thousand-year-old runic song coming back out of the machines as acid house, while Aleksander Sprohgis’ lights, pinned to the beat, cracked across II Kirsimägi every time the bassline turned over and Raho Aadla danced it out at the front of the stage. OOPUS bill themselves as folk on acid and mean it to the letter: the bagpipe drone sat under a squelching acid line as though it had been waiting a millennium for exactly that, with their latest Reivlender playing as one long build. By mid-set a crowd that had spent the day watching thumb pianos and kannels was going properly, sweatily off, the oldest material on the whole bill turned into the closest thing Viljandi had to a nightclub. After midnight the festival split its mood in two. Kaevumägi turned inward for Kuula Hetke, the flute duo of Kärt Pihlap and Katariina Tirmaste, whose name translates as “listen to the moment” and whose method lives up to it: they take melodies from the home regions of their great-grandparents, Mulgimaa and Võrumaa, thread their own writing through them, and pull the whole thing apart and back together on stage. Two flutes, voice and electronics built into slow, elemental soundscapes, and beside them the visual artist Okeiko painted a video world in real time, improvising brushstrokes to match every shift in the music. The Song Festival Grounds went the other way, loud and communal, as Tuulebant+ marked ten years with a birthday set. What began as a handful of young Estonian lads deciding to play together has become a fixture of the dance floors, acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and lõõts (the Estonian button accordion) under four voices, driving the kind of brisk, folk-rooted dance music that owes a clear debt to Untsakad and the Kukerpillid before them. For the anniversary they swelled the core band out with guests borrowed from other line-ups across the weekend, the plus in the name doing real work, and sent the last of the night’s crowd home dancing. Sunday came in warm and dry and ended wringing wet. The early afternoon on I Kirsimägi got a soft landing from Tell Your Birds, an Estonian, Latvian and Italian quartet who assemble their music from old tapes and Baltic tunes, running Estonian and Latvian folk melodies and field-recorded voices through electronics into long, drifting drones. Fiddle, bowed lyre and balafon carried the tunes up front while the fourth of them worked synths and effects beneath, turning a grey start into something to wake up slowly to.  By late afternoon, the sun had pulled the crowd onto Kaevumägi for Nancy Vieira, who brought Cape Verde to Viljandi, and morna to the festival for the first time in its history. Widely seen as the heir to Cesária Évora, Vieira carries that same slow, aching island sound. Born in Guinea-Bissau to Cape Verdean parents before moving to Lisbon at 14, she embodies the exact displacement morna is written about: the voice of the person who left. Backed only by guitar, cavaquinho, light percussion, and her own cool, unhurried lead, her set folded fado, Brazilian rhythms, and West African lines into songs from her 2024 album Gente. Then came the shift: for the final numbers, she invited the crowd right up onto the stage, turning the show into a full-tilt dance through the fast, bouncing tunes of Ano Nobo. The set the weekend had quietly been saving arrived that evening, and it went to Amy Laurenson. She had barely made the festival at all, held up by flight delays, cancellations, and baggage mishandling alongside guitarist Miguel Girão, reaching Viljandi just minutes before their Saturday slot on Kaevumägi in the rain and wind. Sunday finally did her justice, placing her at a grand piano inside the Ait. There, the Shetland pianist takes fiddle tunes written for a bow and hands them to the keys as a lead voice rather than accompaniment: reels arriving with their drive intact and their phrasing completely rethought. Out of the weather, the room went dead silent and stayed that way. It was the finest hour of the four days. Fittingly, the last word went to a band from the festival’s own backyard. Angus formed in 2010 out of Viljandi and its Culture Academy, and have spent the sixteen years since turning out a warm, unhurried reggae, ska and dub sung in Estonian, their 2023 record Vibratsioon hailed by Raadio 2 as the flagship of Estonian reggae-rock. Seven of them shut the festival down from the Song Festival Grounds, joined by guest vocalist Sofia-Liis Liiv, playing out into a downpour to a soaked crowd that skanked through the mud and bouncing along to thick dub basslines and hip-hop rhymes. Before the final fade, frontman Anton Ventsel signed the weekend off with a line worth keeping: “Have a good evening, a safe journey home, and folk is forever.” A local band, on the last stage, in the wet, closing a festival their own town has built its name on. Viljandi did not have its biggest year, but it had a better one than that. The man at the hotel desk had the right instinct and the wrong month. The next edition runs 22nd to 25th July 2027, worth writing down now, because he was not wrong about the room either.   The Viljandi Folk Music Festival returns in 2027, running 22nd to 25th July Ticket sales open in December, but keep an eye out HERE   [See image gallery at rhythmpassport.com] The post Event Review: Viljandi Folk Music Festival 2026 (Viljandi, Estonia; Thursday 23rd to Sunday 26th July 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Dutch post-punk project Bragolin has cast a looming shadow across the international darkwave scene. For the past eight years, its music has passed from listener to listener through word of mouth and digital playlists assembled with the care once given to hand-dubbed mixtapes. With about 300,000 monthly Spotify listeners, the band now stands among the Netherlands’ most-listened-to contemporary wave exports, drawing an audience far beyond Utrecht. The band began there in 2013, when Edwin van der Velde transferred a guitar riff intended for his Dutch-language project Zwarte Poëzie onto a newly purchased Bass VI. The instrument changed the riff’s character and, with it, the course of his work. That piece became Into Those Woods, the first Bragolin song and a centerpiece of the 2018 debut, I Saw Nothing Good So I Left. The album has since been repressed six times on vinyl, while the track’s baritone hook carried it beyond ten million streams and onto darkwave dance floors around the world. Van der Velde expanded Bragolin in 2019 through Let Out The Noise Inside, a full-album collaboration with Adam Tristar that brought more electronic production into the project. Synth player Edwin Daatselaar joined the following year, establishing the current live duo; both musicians also play in Zwarte Poëzie. Bragolin has since performed more than one hundred shows across Europe and Latin America, including appearances at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Amphi Festival, Cold Hearted Festival, Extramuralhas, and Kalabalik. The debut has continued to find new listeners as well: seven years after its release, This Grotesque Dance took off on TikTok and is now Bragolin’s most-streamed song, with over 7 million streams on Spotify alone. Bragolin’s third album, I Don’t Like What It Does to Me, retains the Bass VI, organ tones, and dance rhythms at the center of van der Velde’s writing while widening the arrangements with waterphone, synthetic ocean textures, seagull field recordings, strings, and a guitarless piece assembled entirely from layered Clavinets. “Visuals are what draw my attention,” van der Velde says, and references to The Lighthouse, It Follows, The Thing, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers enter these songs as stories of pursuit, artificial replication, surrender, and disappearance. Carrellee joins him on the album’s duet, Feel This Flame Unfold, extending a collaboration that will continue throughout the upcoming North American and European tours. Post-Punk.com spoke with van der Velde about the Nirvana and Björk records that first drew him toward songwriting, growing up beyond Drenthe’s blues and metal scenes, the growth of the Dutch wave underground, and Grauzone’s international role. He also discusses the unlikely longevity of Bragolin’s earliest songs, the backlash surrounding the video for Not All Are Real, the visual rules that keep faces concealed, the band’s first North American tour, and his ambition to develop concept albums and, perhaps one day, a Bragolin film. Bragolin. Photo by Lisanne Lentink Edwin, what were the first records or artists that seized your imagination growing up, and when did listening turn into the desire to write and perform your own music? When I was a kid, I mostly listened to local radio before I got a few pop music cassettes in the early ’90s, which were full of Eurodance. I didn’t care much about music until I discovered alternative music in my mid-teens. Nirvana and Björk were the artists who opened up that world for me. I was fascinated by what felt like the purity of Nirvana’s music, while Björk showed me how unconventional and unique an artist could be. Nevermind, Unplugged, and Post were the first three albums I owned. For most of those later teenage years, I listened almost exclusively to Nirvana. That inspired me to buy a guitar and start writing songs. You can still hear Nirvana’s influence beneath the surface in my music, in the song structures, the desire to write catchy melodies, and even in the way I often add the lyrics later in the songwriting process. Which books and writers had the strongest effect on you during those formative years? Were there particular novels that shaped Bragolin’s fascination with isolation, dread, and the uncanny? I’ve never been much of a reader. I have difficulty focusing on black letters on a white page. Visuals are what draw my attention. While I’m trying to translate the words into images, my mind often drifts off into its own story. I suddenly realize I’m no longer reading the text and have to go back and start again. It’s rare that I truly enjoy reading. So films have had a much bigger influence on me. It’s a shame, because all my life I’ve heard people say that books are so much more interesting than the films. Bragolin’s music and videos seem to draw from post-apocalyptic and horror cinema, including Gothic and folk horror, science-fiction paranoia, body horror, and cosmic horror. Which films first opened those worlds to you, and what do you tend to take from them—the setting, pacing, imagery, or emotional psychology? As a teenager, I was a big fan of the Terminator and Predator films. My dad has always loved action movies, so I grew up watching a lot of the classics with him. Later on, I discovered arthouse cinema, which gradually introduced me to folk horror. The Village (2004) and The Witch (2015) are great examples of the kind of settings and atmosphere I enjoy. I’m especially drawn to the vulnerability of the main character and the mystery and ambiguity of whatever they’re up against. I like to focus on that tension in my lyrics instead of the gore, although I enjoy those films as well. How did growing up in the Netherlands shape your musical imagination? Are there aspects of the Dutch landscape, culture, or temperament that have found their way into Bragolin? I don’t think growing up in the Netherlands consciously shaped Bragolin very much. I grew up in the province of Drenthe, where blues and metal were pretty much the only music scenes around. That made me realize quite early on that I had to look elsewhere to find like-minded people. Having said that, Dutch folklore is something I’d love to explore one day. I think it could make a great concept album. How would you describe the Dutch post-punk and darkwave scene today? Does it possess a character distinct from the scenes you have encountered elsewhere in Europe and Latin America? The Dutch wave scene has improved enormously over the last decade. It’s still a smaller and somewhat more reserved scene compared to our neighbouring countries, but it’s definitely moving in the right direction. Thanks to the hard work of promoters, musicians, and a new generation of fans, the scene has become much more hopeful than it was ten years ago. With festivals like Grauzone, Wavefest, and Momentum, we now have events of a high international standard. Artists like Adam Tristar, Raderkraft, Lifeless Past, De Ambassade, Silent Runners, Camy Huot, Pol, and many more are finding international success. A decade ago, the Dutch wave scene was mostly known internationally because Clan of Xymox came from here. Now there’s a much broader and healthier scene. Bragolin performed at Grauzone in The Hague earlier this year. What was that experience like, and what role has Grauzone played in connecting the Dutch underground with the wider international post-punk community? This year marked our second appearance at Grauzone. We were only announced as a last-minute replacement three days before the festival, so it was great to see such an enthusiastic response from the audience. What I enjoy most about Grauzone is seeing people from both the Dutch and international wave scene together, alongside visitors from outside the scene. Grauzone has made the genre much more accessible to people who might never have considered going to a post-punk or darkwave festival before. I think that’s played a huge role in helping the scene grow in the Netherlands and in connecting the Dutch underground with the wider international community. Can you take us back to the creation of “Into Those Woods”? Which arrived first: the baritone melody, the repeating organ hook, the rhythm, or those images of the manor, the swing, and the mysterious book? This is an interesting question because it was actually the very first Bragolin song I wrote. It all started with that guitar riff I originally had in mind for my other project, Zwarte Poëzie, in early 2013. In mid-2013, I bought a Bass VI, and when I tried the riff on that instrument, everything suddenly clicked. That Bass VI sound became the foundation of Bragolin when I decided to start it as a second project later that year. Because most of Zwarte Poëzie’s lyrics had been about my personal life, I wanted Bragolin to explore different themes. After watching The Evil Dead, I wrote the lyrics inspired by the film. Around that time I was also a big fan of the band The Organ and wanted to use an organ sound instead of relying mainly on synths like many darkwave bands. That became another defining element of Bragolin’s sound. “Into Those Woods” has surpassed fourteen million streams and become a modern darkwave classic. When did you first realize the song had taken on a life beyond the debut album, and how has your relationship with it changed since 2018? I started Bragolin without any expectations. We were just focused on making music the way we wanted to and making it as good as possible. Being in Zwarte Poëzie for eight years had taught me that success was difficult to achieve, although we did have some success with De Laatste Dagen as a minor dancefloor hit while I was working on the first Bragolin album. I assumed “Into Those Woods” might be too catchy and sound too clean for the goth scene, but fortunately I was wrong. The interesting thing is that the song’s reach kept growing year after year. Every year it felt like, “Okay, we’ve probably reached the ceiling now,” but it kept growing. What’s even more surprising is that “This Grotesque Dance” suddenly became a TikTok hit this winter, despite already being out there for seven years. Over the past year, it even surpassed “Into Those Woods” as our most streamed song. I’m very happy that our fans have embraced the new album just as much, and that Bragolin has grown beyond that one song. When we play live, it sometimes feels like we’ve already had a great show and then there’s that moment of, “Oh wait, we still have this song to come.” When you begin writing a Bragolin song now, what form does the first idea usually take? Could you walk us through the process of developing that fragment into a finished arrangement? For me, having a strong hook on top of a danceable beat and bassline is the foundation. I usually put on a drumbeat and play my Bass VI for hours until I find a riff that I like. I then record it and put it aside for weeks or even months. Listening back to a collection of these basic ideas later makes it easier to distinguish which ones have the most potential. After choosing the strongest one, I develop the riff into a song, often starting by humming vocal lines and eventually replacing those with rough lyrics. I then develop those lyrics into a story, which can be inspired by films I’ve recently watched. After that, I layer the song with additional instruments and sound recordings. On the latest album, I put more focus on that layering process than on the first two albums. For the next album, I would like to focus more on having strong foundations again, similar to the approach I took on the first album. “I Run and Hide” sounds heavily guitar-driven, yet its entire instrumental body was constructed from layered Clavinets. How did you record and process those layers, and what did that self-imposed limitation allow you to discover? After the second album, I bought a bunch of new instruments to embrace creativity. One of them was a small electric piano with different sounds built into it. For this song, I ran it through my Bass VI setup, which is why it doesn’t sound too far removed from the way the Bass VI normally sounds. Because it was a piano sound, I wanted to arrange it as if it could actually be played as a piano piece, with a low bass melody and multiple high melodies. I wanted it to feel like one instrument was playing the whole piece. It showed me that by limiting myself to one sound, I could still create a full arrangement with its own character. I Don’t Like What It Does to Me also incorporates field recordings, synthetic ocean textures, waterphones, and other unconventional sources. Could you identify a few moments where those sounds appear and explain how you manipulated them? For this album, I wanted it to have a more cinematic feel. One of the instruments I started using was the waterphone, which is often used in film scores and sound effects. It appears at various moments throughout the album, but it is especially noticeable at the beginning of the title track and This Presence Like a Breeze. This cinematic approach is also why I used a string section at the beginning of “Not All Are Real” to somewhat recreate the feeling of the opening of The Thing (2011), which is a prequel to the classic 1982 film. There are also two songs with ocean-inspired sounds: “Tar With Salt Foam” and “I Salute You Ancient Ocean”. For both songs, I created the sound of ocean waves with my Korg MS-20 by using synthesis rather than recordings of actual waves, while the seagulls were recorded as field recordings. I then processed and layered these sounds into the arrangements to create the atmosphere I was looking for. Where do your lyrics usually begin—with a personal experience, an image, a line from a book, or a scene from a film? How do you turn an outside reference into something that carries your own emotional meaning? It usually starts with a hummed vocal line, and then I look for words that fit the sounds and rhythm of that melody. From there, a few words become the basis of the lyrics. While watching films, I write down how I experience them visually and emotionally from the perspective of the protagonist. But I don’t want to create a direct interpretation of the film. It is more a starting point for my own lyrics, and often I turn it into my own story rather than sticking to the original inspiration. Which artists working in the current post-punk, darkwave, or experimental underground are exciting you most at the moment? Are there any Dutch acts in particular that you believe deserve a much wider audience? My listening has always been broader than just post-punk and darkwave, but from time to time I return to these genres, and there are still artists within the scene that I find very inspiring. I was pleasantly surprised by Carrellee’s music when she joined our record label, Young & Cold Records, with her self-titled 2025 album. I ended up listening to that album on repeat, which led to us getting in contact, collaborating on songs, and working together on upcoming tours. Other artists within our genre that I’ve been enjoying lately are Grundeis, The Woken Trees, The Soft Moon, Boy Harsher, Dead Man’s Bones, and Murder by Death. However, I have mainly been listening to a lot of 60s music, from Ennio Morricone and The Shadows to Nancy Sinatra and Roy Orbison. It is still often dark and melancholic music, and I think I know what elements to take from other genres and what to leave behind when creating my own music. Bragolin’s videos have become an important extension of the songs, from the manor and woodland imagery of “Into Those Woods” to the nocturnal pursuit through streets and cornfields in “I Run and Hide.” How closely involved are you in developing those concepts, and what do you look for in a director? I usually create at least one music video per album myself. For the others, when looking for a director or editor, the most important thing is that they understand the music, respect our visual identity, and have a fitting portfolio. With the new album, I wanted to create more original footage instead of reusing existing material as on previous albums. My role is mainly setting guidelines, such as avoiding showing faces clearly in our visual content. We call this anonymity. This connects with our album covers, which are all portraits shot from behind, and our lyrics, where we also leave room for interpretation rather than explaining everything too clearly. I Run and Hide was made by two very talented film students, Maria Gaedcke and Jonathan Eder. It was our first time working with a larger production. My idea was to combine the inspiration for the song, the film It Follows (2014), with the new album cover’s figure in the nightgown, while taking the opposite approach to the film by not showing the antagonist explicitly. The video for “Feel This Flame Unfold” was created by State of Poison, who had caught our attention with several great animated productions. Animation offered a chance to explore another style, and I’m really happy with how all the videos turned out. For “Not All Are Real,” you connected The Thing and Invasion of the Body Snatchers with contemporary anxiety about artificial replication, using intentionally unnatural AI-generated imagery. What creative and ethical boundaries did you establish for that video, and did the response to it alter your view of the technology? Even though it received quite a lot of negative responses, I still think the concept I wanted to create was only possible in this way. The video is about artificial replication, so using AI-generated imagery became part of the concept itself rather than just a production tool. Filming people in public without their consent would have raised ethical concerns. Emptying the streets of major cities around the world to create a film set and hiring hundreds of actors simply isn’t realistic within the budget of an independent band. Animation, on the other hand, wouldn’t have captured the unsettling feeling of cloned humans that I was looking for. The only real alternative would have been to abandon the concept and make a completely different video. I also found it interesting that we’d previously used existing footage in our videos, which raises ethical questions of its own, yet that never received the same criticism. That said, the reaction was enough for me to decide: never again. Bragolin will embark on its first North American tour this fall. What are you most looking forward to experiencing on this run, and when you look beyond it, where would you like to take Bragolin next—musically, visually, and geographically? We have had a following in North America for a long time, and the requests for us to come over have gone unanswered for many years. I’m mainly looking forward to finally meeting those fans who have been following us from the beginning and hopefully giving them the show they’ve been waiting for. Looking beyond this tour, I’d like Bragolin to remain a constant by continuing to make albums for many years to come. I’d also love to explore the possibility of creating concept albums, which is an element from the past I’d like to bring back to the present, and combine that with even more visual storytelling, perhaps one day creating our own dedicated film. Geographically, there are still plenty of places we haven’t visited. In early 2027, we’re planning a West Coast tour and a return to Latin America.§ Listen to I Don’t Like What It Does To Me below and order the album here. I Don’t Like What It Does To Me by Bragolin Looking towards the horizon, Edwin Van der Velde hopes to expand Bragolin through future concept albums and, eventually, a film devoted to the project’s visual world. Yet, the immediate priority is Bragolin’s first North American tour. Van der Velde and synth player Edwin Daatselaar will take the band on the road alongside Carrellee for the thirty-date North American Hope Tour, beginning September 3 at X-Ray Arcade in the Milwaukee area. Bragolin has maintained a substantial North American audience for years, yet these will be the duo’s first performances on the continent. The route continues through the Midwest, Ontario and Quebec, the Northeast, the South, and Texas before ending October 11 in Tulsa. Bragolin then returns to Europe for dates beginning October 31 in Utrecht and running through December 19 in Brussels, followed by São Paulo and Santiago in February 2027. A separate West Coast tour is also being planned for early 2027, though its dates have yet to be announced. The schedule reflects the unusual way Bragolin’s audience has grown. Into Those Woods accumulated listeners steadily until it passed ten million streams, while This Grotesque Dance found a new audience through TikTok seven years after its release and eventually became Bragolin’s most-streamed song. Those songs reached North America well before the band could follow them. After years of requests from listeners across the continent, van der Velde and Daatselaar will finally meet that audience in person this fall. items.body: Swedish electro artist EMMON released “Relics (Agent Side Grinder Remix)” on 14 August 2026 through Icons Creating Evil Art. The track is the third remix issued ahead of “ICONMIXED”, a remix album scheduled for 23 October 2026. Jimmy Monell produced and mixed the new version, Hans Olsson mastered it, and Emma Nylén is credited as writer. The original “Relics” is the eighth track on “ICON“, the album EMMON released on 17 October 2025 with Emanuel Åström as guestvocalist. Agent Side Grinder move it off its EBM footing and into house tempo, adding LinnDrum programming, a Euro-disco riff and acid basslines. Johan Lange of Agent Side Grinder set out what the duo changed: “Had a great time remixing my dear friend Emmon (and a certain obscure guest singer). I took the EBM-driven original and pushed it in a more ’90s house direction, with LinnDrum, a Euro disco riff and plenty of acid basslines.” Two reworkings of “Speak to Me” preceded it, one by SIIE and one by Copenhagen trio The Foreign Resort. “ICONMIXED” reworks material from “ICON” across a wider set of collaborators. Icons Creating Evil Art issued an official video for the original “Relics” the same day. Niklas Kärreskog directed it, with Tyko Lann Lundin as editing assistant and Joakim Kärreskog on technical resources. Kärreskog set out his reference points in the video credits: “Relics could easily be part of the soundtrack to a film adaptation of William Gibson’s Neuromancer. That’s why I aimed for a cyberpunk aesthetic inspired by Ridley Scott’s Alien (1979) and Shinya Tsukamoto’s Tetsuo (1989). To achieve this, the video was processed through a CRT television and many metres of cable.” EMMON has run this pattern before. “RECON” arrived in 2022 and drew a full companion remix record a year later; “ICONMIXED” applies the same treatment to the newer album. About EMMON EMMON is the solo project of Swedish artist and producer Emma Nylén, based in Stockholm and signed to Icons Creating Evil Art. Her earlier catalogue runs from “The Art and The Evil” and “Closet Wanderings” through “Nomme”, “AON” and “Under Construction”, built on hard synth basslines, clipped vocals and melodic electro structures. “RECON” followed on 7 October 2022 and reopened that catalogue after an extended gap. Its eleven tracks include “Machines”, “Like A Drum” and “Purebloods”, a duet with Agent Side Grinder vocalist Emanuel Åström that set up the working relationship behind the current remix. On 6 October 2023 EMMON issued “RECONMIXED”, a thirteen-track companion that handed “Machines”, “Reconstruction”, “Purebloods” and others to Ultra Sunn, Tobias Bernstrup, Sex Kino, Harlem, Fred White, Maschine Brennt, Majestoluxe, ZackZackZack, Potochkine and Livmødr. The “XCEPTION” EP came next, then “ICON” on 17 October 2025, a ten-track album covering “Neon Brown”, “Decisions”, “Shades of Blue”, “Cold Within”, “No Mans Land”, “Speak to Me”, “Blood on the Ceiling feat. Majestoluxe”, “Relics”, “DARK” and “Slow Running”. Icons Creating Evil Art issued it on vinyl, CD and digital. Side-Line covered that release and published an EMMON interview in February 2026. The rollout toward “ICONMIXED” started with SIIE and The Foreign Resort on “Speak to Me” and continues with Agent Side Grinder on “Relics”. The album is due on 23 October 2026.
items._cn_summary: 本文为新闻报道性质，介绍瑞典电子音乐人EMMON与Agent Side Grinder合作的混音单曲。混音版本将原曲的EBM基底转向九十年代浩室律动，加入LinnDrum鼓机编程、欧陆迪斯科旋律线与酸性贝斯线条。报道同时交代了即将发行的混音合辑背景，列出此前两首混音作品的合作者，并梳理了EMMON的创作脉络与厂牌归属。官方MV采用赛博朋克美学，致敬《神经漫游者》小说氛围，结合《异形》与《铁男》的视觉处理，经CRT电视与电缆进行画面处理。内容以信息发布为主，缺乏对音乐本身的深度评析与听觉描述。

items.body: London-based queer alt-metal artist Ray Noir releases “Gothstar” on 13 August 2026, a rave-metal single featuring New York alternative artist Danny Blu. The track is the final single ahead of Ray Noir’s second EP, also titled “Gothstar,” scheduled for 17 September 2026. A label, catalogue number and full tracklist for the EP have not been confirmed. Ray Noir “Gothstar” EP release date and earlier singles The “Gothstar” EP is scheduled for 17 September 2026 and follows three 2026 singles building up to the EP release. “Label Whxre” arrived on 2 April 2026, the release on which Kerrang! reported the EP as a “rave meets metalcore” record. “Black” followed on 14 May 2026, produced by Jon Cass and written with Tom Saint. “Boys” was issued as the third single. KALTBLUT magazine reported in April 2026 that the EP would include a collaboration with Danny Blu without naming the track, and now the 13 August release confirms that collaboration as the title track. “Gothstar” The single combines techno, metalcore and rave production. Promotional material for the release describes the track as moving from the Berlin club Berghain “straight into the mosh pit,” and frames its themes as goth glamour, queer confidence and self-expression. “Gothstar” is also the name of the character at the centre of the EP, and the EP’s title track. Ray Noir released an official music video with the single. Both artists of course appropriately in black leather 😉 “Gothstar” release party in London Ray Noir will host a free release party at Slim Jim’s Liquor Store in London on 19 September 2026. Tickets are listed via DICE. About Ray Noir Ray Noir is a queer alternative artist based in London. According to his official biography, his background is in Oslo’s black-metal underground, and his sound combines metal guitars with electronic club production. He began releasing solo material with the single “Double Trouble” in 2014 and has since worked with a range of underground collaborators. His 2024 mixtape “Scorpio” reached the top five of the German Alternative Charts according to his official biography, and drew coverage from Kerrang! and BBC Radio 1. The 2025 EP “Against the Machine” followed and featured guitarist Steve Stevens. In 2026 he released “Temptation” and “Breathe,” then opened the “Gothstar” campaign with “Label Whxre,” “Black” and “Boys.” Live, his official biography lists sold-out headline shows in London and Oslo, multiple UK tours, performances in Tokyo and at Flow Festival in Finland and Resistanz Festival in the UK, and support slots for Combichrist and Die Krupps. His work in fashion, including with Marc Jacobs and Vivienne Westwood, was cited by KALTBLUT magazine as an influence on “Label Whxre.” No Wikipedia article for Ray Noir surfaced during verification, and Discogs did not return a matching profile, so discography formats and catalogue numbers could not be cross-checked. About Danny Blu Danny Blu is an alternative artist based in New York and the former frontman of Echo Black. He relaunched his solo project with the single “Bubble” in 2019 and released the EPs “The Pale Horse” and “Molotov” in 2021. “Gothstar” is his first confirmed recorded collaboration with Ray Noir.
items._cn_summary: 这篇内容是一则关于单曲发布的新闻稿，介绍了Ray Noir与Danny Blu合作的单曲《Gothstar》，作为其第二张EP的先行单曲发布。这首歌将techno、metalcore与rave制作手法相融合，官方宣传将其定位为从柏林Berghain俱乐部直接切入mosh pit的体验，主题围绕哥特魅力、酷儿自信与自我表达。Ray Noir的音乐背景融合了奥斯陆黑金属的吉他音色与电子俱乐部制作，体现出暗潮与工业领域常见的跨界实验倾向。《Gothstar》作为EP同名曲，承载了整体概念叙事的核心。文章本身更多是信息性发布而非深度乐评，缺乏对声音设计、制作细节或音乐结构的深入分析。

items.body: Hocico‘s debut full-length album, “Odio Bajo El Alma,” turns 29 on 14 August. The Mexican electro-industrial duo released the record on 14 August 1997 through the Mexican label Opción Sónica, with European distribution handled by Out Of Line. ‘Odio Bajo El Alma’ tracklist and credits “Odio Bajo El Alma” was Hocico’s first official release after three self-produced cassette demos – “Misuse, Abuse and Accident” (1993), “Autoagresión Persistente” (1994) and “Triste Desprecio” (1996). The album was produced by Edmundo Navas, with engineering handled by the band alongside Rogelio Gómez. It was issued on CD and cassette in Mexico, later reissued in Germany through Out Of Line and Sub/Mission Records, and reissued again on vinyl by Out Of Line in 2019. The album runs 11 tracks: “Cuando la Maldad Despierta” “Odio en el Alma” “Beings of Relief” “Final Resource” “Hell on Earth” “Gota de Sangre” “Temple of Lies” “Sexo Bajo Testosterona (Frenetik Mix ’96)” “Sad Scorn” “Slow Death” “Face to Face” The record is available to stream via Spotify. According to Wikipedia, “Odio Bajo El Alma” was well received across Europe and the Americas and introduced audiences outside Mexico to a style of electronic music few realized was being made there. Before the album’s release, Hocico had been part of a Mexico City collective called La Corporación, alongside acts such as Cenobita, Ogo, Encefálisis and Deus Ex Machina, that supported and promoted the country’s electronic underground. About Hocico Hocico is a Mexican electro-industrial duo formed in 1993 in Mexico City by cousins Eric García, performing as Erk Aicrag, and Óscar Mayorga, performing as Racso Agroyam. García writes the lyrics and performs vocals, while Mayorga handles programming. Both had experimented with electronic music since their teens, drawing on industrial acts such as Skinny Puppy. Their musical partnership began in 1989 in a group called Niñera Degenerada, and in 1992 the two left that project to form Hocico de Perro, later shortened simply to Hocico. Between 1993 and 1996 the duo self-released three cassette demos before issuing “Odio Bajo El Alma” in 1997 on Opción Sónica with Out Of Line handling European distribution. The end of the decade brought the live album “Los Hijos Del Infierno,” recorded during Hocico’s 1998 European tour, and the studio follow-up “Sangre Hirviente” (1999), which reached number 19 on the CMJ RPM chart in the United States. Hocico played the Zillo festival in Germany and the Euro Rock festival in Belgium in 1999, returned to Germany’s Woodstage festival in 2000 in front of more than 20,000 people, and opened for Rammstein during that band’s 2001 Mexican tour. “Signos De Aberración” followed in 2002, then “Wrack And Ruin” in 2004, after which the band paused new studio material. During the break, García launched his solo project Rabia Sorda and relocated to Leipzig, Germany, while Mayorga remained based in Mexico City. Hocico resumed with “Memorias Atrás” in 2008 and has released an album roughly every two years since: “Tiempos de Furia” (2010), “El Ultimo Minuto” (2012), “Los días caminando en el fuego” (2013), “Ofensor” (2015), “The Spell of the Spider” (2017, which reached number 42 on the German national charts) and “Artificial Extinction” (2019, an album centered on artificial intelligence as a threat to humanity, which peaked at number 30 in Germany). “Hyperviolent” followed in 2022. Side-Line has continued to track the band’s output, including the Hey Tú EP expansion with Prayers and, most recently, the ‘Unseen Horror Scenes’ album, released in May 2026. Twenty-nine years after “Odio Bajo El Alma” introduced the duo to audiences outside Mexico, the album remains the starting point of that catalog.
items._cn_summary: 墨西哥电子工业双人组Hocico于1997年通过Opción Sónica厂牌发行首张全长专辑《Odio Bajo El Alma》，由Out Of Line负责欧洲分销。这张专辑在发行三盘自制磁带Demo后诞生，制作人为Edmundo Navas，收录11首曲目，涵盖西语与英语交替的工业电子作品。乐队在此前参与了墨西哥城的La Corporación地下电子集合，与Cenobita、Deus Ex Machina等团体共同推动本土电子地下场景的发展。作为将墨西哥电子工业音乐引入欧美听众视野的早期作品，专辑融合了Skinny Puppy式工业噪音影响与拉丁美洲地下场景的粗粝质感，歌词与节奏编程由Erk Aicrag和Racso Agroyam两位表兄弟分工完成。2019年由Out Of Line再版黑胶，曲目现可通过Spotify流媒体收听。

items.body: German electronic composer Volker Rapp released “Silent Running” on 14 August 2026 through the Argentine label Cyclical Dreams. The 18-track album follows the narrative of Douglas Trumbull’s 1972 science-fiction film of the same name, and is out digitally and as a CD edition. Rapp traces the project back more than fifty years. He states: “Silent Running has been one of my favorite films ever since I saw it on German television on April 26, 1974.” How Volker Rapp built ‘Silent Running’ The tracklist reads as a synopsis. It opens with “The last forests of Earth” and “The arks Berkshire, Valley Forge, Sequoia and Mojave”, introduces “Freeman Lowell, gardener and guardian”, then moves through “Daily Routine”, “Service robots Dewey, Huey and Louie”, “Order to destroy the domes”, “What are we doing here”, “Lonely Decision #1”, “Realising the Domes”, “Silent Running to Saturn”, “The Lord of the Rings”, “Through the Rings and Louie is lost”, “Berkshire is calling”, “Remorse”, “Lonely Decision #2”, “Preparing the Last Dome and Dewey”, “Valley Forge and Lowell are lost” and “Infinity”. Those titles track the film closely. In Trumbull’s picture, Bruce Dern plays botanist Freeman Lowell, who tends the last of Earth’s forests in domes aboard the freighter Valley Forge near Saturn, assisted by three service drones he names Huey, Dewey and Louie. Trumbull had supervised the special photographic effects on “2001: A Space Odyssey” in 1968; “Silent Running” was the first of only two features he directed, the other being “Brainstorm” in 1983. He died on 7 February 2022. Rapp built the record around period-correct instrumentation, working with the ARP 2600 and SEM alongside a Juno 6, Prophet 5, MS-20, DX7 and Synclavier, plus Arturia software. He is explicit that the album stands on its own rather than functioning as a replacement score, noting: “This version is not synchronized with the film; it runs 73 minutes compared to 85 minutes in the 2002 DVD version.” Silent Running [CYD 0164] by vOLKER rAPP Cyclical Dreams handled the artwork; Amp Puttipong supplied the photography. About Volker Rapp Volker Rapp was born on 10 October 1964 in Wuppertal, Germany, and works as a composer, musician, photographer and writer. He ran the Demo Art project from 1992 to 2005 and has also recorded as part of the duo Volker & Volker. His recent output has come almost entirely through Cyclical Dreams, the Buenos Aires label founded in early 2020 by Pablo Bilbao, Lucas Tripaldi and Esteban Menash, which concentrates on Berlin School, ambient, soundscape, space music and drone. Rapp’s titles for the label include “d7-d5” in March 2023, “Blade Runner 2099” in July 2024 and “Phase IV”. Earlier self-released records include “Mars Missions 2021”, issued in February 2021, along with “Declination”, “DUNE Spots”, “Valletta (il-Belt)”, “St. Petersburg” and “Session 8 – My Tribute to Klaus Schulze”. Film and space themes run through most of that catalogue, and Cyclical Dreams has released comparable long-form work by other artists in the same field, including D*Time’s “Nightwoven” in May 2026 and Christian Wittman’s “Andromeda” in January 2026. “Silent Running” is Rapp’s longest sequence for the label to date and his most direct treatment of a single film.
items._genre: electronic / ambient / Berlin School / synth / space music
items._cn_summary: 德国电子音乐人Volker Rapp以1972年科幻电影《Silent Running》为蓝本，创作了18首曲目、73分钟的概念专辑。整张唱片并非电影配乐的重制，而是以独立叙事结构呈现。Rapp使用ARP 2600、SEM、Prophet 5、Juno 6、MS-20、DX7、Synclavier等合成器，搭配Arturia软件，复刻七十年代模拟合成器的音色质感。曲目命名严格遵循电影情节线，从地球最后的森林到主角Lowell的孤独旅程，每一首歌对应一个叙事节点。这种叙事驱动的方式使专辑更像一部听觉化的电影剧本。专辑由阿根廷独立厂牌Cyclical Dreams发行，专注柏林学派、环境音、太空音乐等小众领域，凸显了其地下厂牌属性。

items.body: （13）遠方より無へ（Ⅱ）『レオス』の「眺め」〜水は水 Text by 丘山万里子（Mariko Okayama） 『レオス』（1976）での仏教的「永遠への回帰という死の安らぎ」「無、空へのいざない」から、なぜ突如、ドイツ現象学を援用した『ノエシス』へ飛んだのか？ その経緯は、『レオス』の自作解説に示されている。三善は『レオス』京都初演後の自分を想像し、こう述べる。 「寒気と寂寥の古都のどこかで、灯と酒に寄りそい、たった今自分を分裂させた十数分の異常感覚が、やがて津波のようにあらぬ形で襲ってくるのにおびえながら、自分の、軽口と無口の不器用な連鎖をもてあましているに違いない」。（『遠方より無へ』p.158） そうしてその寒気に、十数年前に訪れた冬のアムステルダムを想い出す。青春期、彼が愛したカミュが事故死（1960）して間もない頃のこと。港近くの酒場の扉を押し、港内にいくつか船影の見える窓辺で三善はジュニエーブル（杜松酒）を注文、『転落』（カミュ作）の冒頭シーン、アムステルダムのバー「メキシコ・シティー」の片隅へとまぎれ込むのだ。 「アルジェの太陽を血のなかに宿したために、ついには古典的な実存主義の矛盾律のなかに回帰せざるをえなかったカミュを『転落』の忘れがたい一句をつぶやくことで私なりに葬（とむら）う心算もあったかもしれないが。――A Moins vous ne m’authorisiez à plaider votre cause, il ne devinera pas que vous desirez du genièvre.」(同上) 『転落』の前後の文脈からこの一句、「私に代弁を任せてくれないと、あなたがジュニエーブルを所望であることを彼は察知できないでしょう」とでも訳しておく。主人公たる「告解者にして裁判官」のクラマンスが、バーを訪れた旅人に語りかけるこのセリフは、オランダ語しか解さないゴリラ（gorille：文明と野蛮の文脈だ）のような店の主人の紹介に次いで出てくる。 三善はなぜこのセリフを、その胸に忘れがたく刻んでいたのか。 『転落』は、かつてパリで栄光に満ちた弁護士生活を送っていたクラマンスが、小雨ふる晩秋の深夜、セーヌに落ちた女の叫び声を耳にしながらその場を去った時から始まる転落人生を旅人相手に語るもの。何度も聞こえながら遠去かり、やがてぷつりと声の消えたしじまで、彼の頭に浮かんだのは「もう遅すぎる、もう間に合わない……」。 小説の最終節で、彼は旅人が同業の弁護士と知り、頼むのだ。自分の頭をぐるぐる回り続けている言葉、「おお、うら若き娘よ、もう一度水の中に飛び込んでくれ！そうすれば今一度、私たち二人ともを救い出す機会が持てるんだ！」（『転落』前山悠新訳、p.181）を、彼の口から言って欲しい、と。小説冒頭、旅人の代弁者となることを提案したクラマンスは、最後、同業者に代弁を請うている。だが、その最後のセリフは、「もう遅すぎるんです。今となっては、そしてこれからもずっと手遅れのままです。幸いなことに！」(同上、p.181)。 そこに口をあけるのは、カミュその人の抱える魂の空洞、私もあなたも永遠の地獄の円環、底なしの実存苦に堕ちてゆくのだ、という絶望で、若い三善はそれを我がものと感じていたのだろう。アムステルダムの同心円状の河が「地獄の円環」（ダンテ『神曲』）そっくりだ、というくだりでの「ブルジョワの地獄、悪しき夢がふんだんに詰め込まれた」それ、「外からやって来た者は同心円の内側へとひとつひとつ踏み入っていく。それにつれ、問われる人生の罪は色濃く、どす黒いものへと変わっていく。そして今わたしたちがたどり着いたのは最後の円。(後略）」(同上、p.24~25) 最後の地獄の円の行き止まりは、かつての三善の希死願望の描く放物線の終着点でもあったろう。 だが、忘れがたい一句の後に続くのは、『転落』の実存地獄を我がものと感じていた自身への疑念だ。 「こうして、死は、生の末端で小さい輝きを放つ出来事のように、私には思われていた。 だが、はたしてそうだろうか。」 そうして2年前の初秋、母を焼く煙が山肌を伝い云々の「永遠への回帰という死の安らぎ」へと想いは流れてゆく。 『レオス』解説におけるこの転回は、1971年に書かれた以下の一文にも示されている。 「かつて死は選ぶことのできるものと思っていた。生の毎瞬を選ぶように。それが、生きることの最も明白なあかしになるのだし、と。（中略）私たちは、生まれてしまったことで死を予約し、毎日の生でこれを分割払いし続け、やがて人生の最期に支払い終えたものを手中にする。それならば、“それ”を与えられるのではなく、どのような形であれ自分の意志により自分の手で、創れないものだろうか――せめて、そうして永遠の時間のなかの人間的な一点として。」 だが続けて、「けれどもいったい、一個の人間の即自性などは、カミュもそこへ堕ちてしまった＜我思う、ゆえに我あり＞の小さな循環を出るものではあるまい。」「自殺もまた、自然の摂理の、ほんの微細な塵埃なのだ。」（『遠方より無へ』―生の最高の瞬間―p.173~174） 『レオス』より5年、『レクイエム』より1年早く、ここに三善の生と死の転回点、即ちカミュと共震する自身の西欧的実存意識への懐疑が示されている。おそらく『王孫不帰』(1970)で能の謡へと心が動いたのも、それ。続く『オデコのこいつ』（1971）での「この子はボク」という自覚にこそ、観念的実存論の空疎が三善の中で顕在化したのだ、と言えよう。日々伝わる60年代半ばからのベトナム戦争、ビアフラの悲劇の生々しさに、世界苦（人間苦）はかつても今も、等しく在る。「これも、ボクの日常だった…….。」ゆえこそ『レクイエム』（1972）の「葬い」を、生者のあいだに限られる、と自ら厳しく峻別した。 『転落』のあちこちに散らばる「rien」と「néant」は、セーヌの川底に流れる実存主義の矛盾律の通奏低音であったろう。カミュはサルトルの実存と相容れなかったが、三善は「出来のいいサルトルのイマジネールよりも、失敗したカミュの古典的な絶望を愛していた。」（同上、p.210） サルトルの『嘔吐』にもまた、「rien」と「néant」が並ぶ。主人公ロカンタンはマロニエの根の、言葉では言い表せない生のままの黒々とふしくれだった恐ろしい塊に「嘔吐」するが、そこで起きているのは、言語化不能な「何か」の露呈（存在の顕現）に対する人間の表層意識の混濁だ。物語終節でのラグタイム『Some of These Days』の「Some of these days / You’ll miss me, honey…」のメロディはロカンタンの「多少の光明」（『嘔吐』鈴木道彦訳、p.279）ともなるが、三善はそれより転落するクラマンスの絶望を愛した。 だが、カミュであれサルトルであれ、彼らは逃れようなく神（キリスト教世界）をその背に負っている。それが西欧精神文化世界の核心であり、天国も地獄も存在も無も、その世界内での「人間論」（人間とは何か）でしかない。無神論は、有神であってこそ成り立つもの。一方、三善に神は居らず、仏も居ない。「遠方より無へ」という観想は、『王孫不帰』からぼんやりと感触され、作品ごとにそれが膨らんでいったと思える。 であるなら、『シェーヌ』(1973)の「rien」は、もはやカミュやサルトルのそれではなく、三善独自の「rien」（無）であり、けれども未だ見えぬ「何か」であった。 『プロターズ（Protase de loin à rien）』（2台ギターのための/1974）のprotaseを彼は「前景」とし、翌年の『エピターズ（Épitase）』（ギター独奏のための/1975）をギリシア劇の「転」あるいは「変動」と語るが、そのように『レオス』に至る一つ一つが、次第に三善に一つの「眺め」すなわち「遠方より無」を、明らめて行ったのだ。 私がここで「眺め」という言葉を使うのには理由がある。言語学者かつ世界の思想・芸術・宗教全般を広く俯瞰、そこに通底する普遍原理を探究した碩学、井筒俊彦がその著作『意識と本質〜精神的東洋を索（もと）めて』（岩波書店）で言及している日本の古典文学に、「ながめ」の深さを説く一節があるからだ。曰く。 「ながむれば我が心さへはてもなく、行くへも知らぬ月の影かな」「帰る雁過ぎぬる空に雲消えていかに詠めん春の行くかた」（式子内親王）。 月は照り、雲は流れ、飛ぶ雁が視界をかすめる。だがこの詩人の意識はそれらの事物に鋭く焦点を合わせていない。それらは遠い彼方に、限りなく遠いところに「眺め」られている。この「眺め」の焦点をぼかした視線の先で、事物はその「本質」的限定を超える。そこに詩的情緒の纏綿があり、存在深層の開顕がある。「眺め」は一種独特な存在体験、世界に対する意識の独特な関わりである。『新古今』的幽玄追求の雰囲気のさなかで完全に展開し切った形においては、「眺め」の意識とは、むしろ事物の「本質」的規定性を朦朧化して、そこに現成する茫漠たる情趣空間のなかに存在の深みを感得しようとする意識主体的態度ではなかったろうか。 （『意識と本質』p.53~54） 「本質」を対象とする「……の意識」の対象志向性の尖端をできるだけぼかすことにより、「本質」の本来的機能である存在規定性を強度に弱めようとする。井筒の言う古典的日本文化の「眺め」の姿勢とは、これだ。 私は思う。三善の真言「遠方より無へ」こそ、この「眺め」そのものの表象ではないか、と。これは、前回触れたブッダの悟り「十二支縁起」の縁起の連関、仏教で言うところの「あるがまま」を「眺め」て真理を会得する姿勢に通じよう。ついでに言うと、『シェーヌ』のシェーネット（鎖）は、鎖という目に見える「モノ（物）」の一方で、「縁起」という目に見えない働き（作用）をこそ、その音に響かせているように私には聴こえるのだ。だから、「à rien」……。 カミュとサルトルの「rien」と「néant」がそれぞれに何であるか、は私の手にあまる。 「rien」が日常の具体において事物が「何も無いこと」を意味するのに対し、「néant」は哲学概念における「無」あるいは「虚無」である、とは一般論で、カミュとサルトルがこれらにどのようなイメージを持っていたかは哲学・文学の専門家の知見を仰ぎたいが、今は先を急ぐ。現時点では、『シェーヌ』の「rien」はフランス実存主義のそれではなかろう、とだけ。 ここに、カミュの眺め、『転落』に描かれるマルケン島での「まさしく負の風景、その中でも最も美しいもの」を旅人に示すシーンを引いておこう (Ebooks libres et gratuits p.53)。 Voilà, n’est-ce pas, le plus beau des paysages négatifs ! Voyez, à notre gauche, ce tas de cendres qu’on appelle ici une dune, la digue grise à notre droite, la grève livide à nos pieds et, devant nous, la mer couleur de lessive faible, le vaste ciel où se reflètent les eaux blêmes. Un enfer mou, vraiment ! Rien que des horizontales, aucun éclat, l’espace est incolore, la vie morte. N’est-ce pas l’effacement universel, le néant sensible aux yeux ? Pas d’hommes, surtout, pas d’hommes ! Vous et moi, seulement, devant la planète enfin déserte ! 以下、前山悠新訳の要約。 「これぞまさしく負の風景、その中でも最も美しいものと言えましょう！――左手には灰の積もったような砂丘、右手には灰色の堤防、足元には鉛色の砂浜、正面には洗剤を薄めたような色の海、その水の青白さが映り込んだ広大なる空。まったく、しなびた地獄のような風景！ ただ水平線のみ、光はなく、無色なる空間、生命も死に絶えている。全面的な漂白、目に痛いほどの虚無ではありませんか？ 人がいない、そう何よりも人間がいない！ついに空っぽとなったこの星で、いるのはわたしとあなただけ！」（同上、p.93） ここで『遠い帆』の月の浦、海と空と雲を思い浮かべるのは私だけだろうか。長い苦難の旅の果て、帰還した月の浦の浜に立つ支倉常長と三善が眺めたのは、決して「負の風景」でも「しなびた地獄」でもなかった。「正負」を超えた、何か…..。 ともあれ、『変化嘆詠』（1975）で「人間を含めた、弱いものとしての生きものと自然との、いたわりに満ちた合一の図」に心動き、「村人、一休、三変化とも、なんと哀しく、優しいのであろう」と呟く三善は、もはやカミュの負の景色からは抜け出ている。 「若いカミュは、アルジェの旅先で、海や風や太陽との合一を謳う。彼が背負った文明では、自然は日常と対（む）きあっている。―日常の鎖―（1965）」（同上、p.47）「“死”だけがカミュを“もの”に還すことで、合一を許した」（同上、p.209）。 そのように、人間と自然との隔絶に立ち竦む西欧実存主義から離れ、三善の眼差しは、村人も一休も三変化も互いを分け隔てなく一緒くたにくるみ込む「慈悲」に注がれる。対象との合一ではなく自分もまたそこに含まれる溶融感覚、それが生死を分たぬ『レオス』の世界であった。その音景を再び辿ってみよう。 冒頭、しじまから浮かび上がる微小な水泡を思わせるコンチキや貝鳴子の不可思議な響き、広がる幻想。時に薄明、時に玲瓏、時にメロディアス、時に切迫と表情は変わるものの一貫して水は水。一瞬の鳥影、魚影。深山幽谷かつ飛流直下の自在なその姿。打の轟きに瀑布を眺め、飛沫を浴び、引き込まれ、呑み込まれ、はたまた水底（水面ではない）に揺れる月影星影。弦のうにゃうにゃ小蛇行絡み合いのカオスからの追い込み、裂帛ffff。一気に沈潜ののち、一雫一雫から広がる水輪の微細、フラクタルな美。スコアを見ると、三善の求める響きの切実に胸打たれる。終尾、弦の深い保続音にチェレスタが澄明に滴り、遥か彼方、貝鳴子がppで「lontane」（遠い）……。 そう、lontane、だ。                                 前稿では『レオス』を道元の《有時》（うじ）における「永遠の今」としたが、今はそれとは異なる眺めが見える。鎌倉時代の曹洞宗開祖、道元は『正法眼蔵』（彼が会得した仏法の正法・極意・真理の解説書）を著したが、《山水経》は、その中の一つで（《有時》も）、ここでは「水」に関する一節を引いておく。 「仏言く、一切の諸法は畢竟解脱にして、所住有ること無しと。（中略）しかあるに人間の水をみるに、流注（るちゅう）してとどまらざるとみる一途（いちず）あり。その流に多般あり、これ人見（にんけん）の一端なり、いはゆる地を流通（るづう）し、空（くう）を流通し、上方に流通し、下方に流通す。一曲にもながれ、九淵（きゅうえん）にもながる。のぼりて雲をなし、くだりてふちをなす。（中略）しかあれば、仏土のなかに水あるにあらず。水裏（すいり）に仏土あるにあらず。水の所在すでに三際にかかはれず、しかもかくのごとくなりといへども、水現成（みずげんじょう）の公案なり。」（現代語訳『正法眼蔵１』玉城康四郎 p.421） およその意味は、分かろう。 この一文への玉城康四郎による訳文・解説を添えておく。 「ありとあらゆるものは、いかなるものからも解放されていて、束縛はないけれども、しかもそれぞれの境位に安住している。そうであるのに、人間が水を見る場合に、水は流れ流れて止まらない、と見る一方的な見方がある。（後略）」（同上、p.422） あるいは、 「水の道は、水自身が知覚しているのでもなく、また知覚していないのでもないけれども、水は水の道に従って作用しているのである。」 （同上、p.423） これが道元の「眺め」（正法）であり、つまりは見方によって水はどうにでも見えようが、水は水だ。どう姿を変えようと、変わらず水は水だ。 カミュもサルトルも、「我見」（我の意識）で世界に対峙、対象（モノ）の本質（存在）に迫ろうとする。そうして同心円の地獄や、負の風景に絶望し、あるいは言語化不能なマロニエの根に対峙してそのおどろおどろしい黒い塊に嘔吐する。 道元は、「我見」を離れ、ああでもこうでもどうでもそのように「在る」ものはありのまま「在る」のだと心得よ、と説く。坐禅は半眼だが、これは対象に対峙するな、凝視するな、識別するな、分節するな、事物（世界）の輪郭を曖昧にぼんやり眺め、内に向けよ、という指導であろう。 と、こう頭を巡らせると、『レオス』の音の成り行きが、まさに「水は水」と語りかけてくるのである。「水は水」という存在の瀬音が聴こえてくるのである。 ではあるが、三善に「無、空へのいざない」がいかに強い誘惑であったとして、慈悲に溶けたい強い情動があったとして、そうそうたやすく生もなく死もなく、流不流に身を預けられようか。「死」は、戦時の無数の「死者」は、なお彼の眼前に対置され続ける。だが、母は蒼穹に煙となって溶けた。この安心はどこから来るのか？ 三善の煩悶は長かった。 ＊ ＊ ＊ サルトルの『存在と無』（L’Être et le néant） の副題が「現象学的存在論の試み」（Essai d’ontologie phénoménologique）であることを思えば、また、サルトルがフッサールの現象学を学ぶべくベルリンに留学し（1933~1934）、彼の地で『嘔吐』の執筆に取り掛かっていることを思えば、三善が『ノエシス』へゆくのは必然だった。「我思うゆえに我あり」の「我」の「意識」構造を再検討すること。フランス実存主義からドイツ現象学へ、人間の「意識」に改めて向き合うことで、三善は自己検証を試みる。 それが『ノエシス』だ。 『ノエシス』に行くにあたり、サルトルの『嘔吐』のマロニエの根の長い長い一節から、私が気になった箇所を抜き出しておく。マロニエを前にしての吐き気の何たるかについての抜粋である。（『嘔吐』鈴木道彦訳） 「もしも存在とは何かと訊かれたら、私は本気でこう答えただろう。それは何でもない、せいぜい、外から物につけ加わった空虚な形式にすぎず、物の性質を何一つ変えるものではない、と。それから不意に、存在がそこに在った。それは火を見るよりも明らかだった。存在はとつぜんヴェールを脱いだのである。存在は抽象的な範疇に属する無害な様子を失った。それは物の生地そのもので、この根は、存在の中で捏ねられ形成されたのだった。と言うよりもむしろ、根や、公園の鉄柵や、ベンチや、禿げた芝生などは、ことごとく消えてしまった。物の多様性、物の個別性は、仮像にすぎず、表面を覆うニスにすぎない。そのニスは溶けてしまった。あとには怪物じみた、ぶよぶよした、混乱した塊が残った―― むき出しの塊、恐るべき、また猥褻な裸形の塊である。」（p.212） 「存在するとは単に、“そこにある”ということなのだ。存在者は出現し、“出会い”に身を委ねるが、人間は絶対にこれを“演繹”できない。そのことを理解した人もいるだろう。ただし彼らは、必然的な自己原因の存在を作り上げて、この偶然性を乗り越えようと試みたのだ。（中略）存在の偶然性は見せかけでもなく、消し去ることのできる仮象でもない。それは絶対であり、したがって完全な無償性である。すべては無償だ、この公園も、この町も、私自身も。それを理解すると胸がむかむかして、すべてはふわふわと漂い始める。」（p.217~218） 「無償性gratuité」を、私は「根拠のなさ」と捉える（ふと三善の「根こそぎ喪失」を思う）。偶然性、無償性、不条理性（『嘔吐』文中より）など、説明できない状況、剥き出しの「存在」に出会った、触れた驚愕、不気味、不快による吐き気を、井筒は『意識と本質』で、こう述べる（適宜私的解釈と要約 p.4~20）。 人間は常日頃、感覚、知覚、意志、欲望、思惟などからなる「表層意識」によって「本質」を認知しようとし（これは「公園の」「マロニエの」「根」だ云々探求）自分を取り巻く世界の安定（構築）に努めるが、その意識レベルで捉え得ないところにこそ「存在の絶対無分節的真相」の深淵がある。 東洋の精神的伝統はこの絶対無分節の「存在」に直面しても狼狽しない。東洋の哲人は深層意識が拓かれ、そこに身を据え表層意識次元の事物、様態を深層の地平に置く。ゆえ、表層・深層の両領域にわたり、絶対無分節の「存在」と、千々に分節された「存在」とが、同時にありのままに現れている、と捉える。 禅者の「山はこれ山、水はこれ水」とは、無数の「本質」によってさまざまに区切られ、複雑に聯関し合う「本質」の網目を通して分節的に眺める地平と同時に、無分節の存在の無数のさざめきをあるがままに眺める地平（本質なき「無」、自律なき「無自性」）とを併せ持つ、表層深層からの語り出し。「深層意識と表層意識とを二つながら同時に機能させることによって、“存在”の無と有とをいわば二重写に観ることのできる」、それが東洋的哲人の姿勢（p.14）。 この深層意識を体験的事実として認めるのが東洋哲学一般の根本的な一つの特徴で、前回のブッダの十二支縁起（全ては関係性）と重なろう。なお、井筒は東洋だけでなく、プロティノス（エジプト生まれ 205? – 270）の説く「一者 to hen」（「有」の彼方、「実在性」の彼方、「思考力」の彼方なるもの、すなわち言詮の彼方なる絶対窮極者）もまた「厳密に言えば、“かのもの”とも“このもの”とも言ってはならないのである。どんな言葉を使ってみても、我々はそれの外側を、むなしく駆け廻っているだけのことだ」と、存在の本源的無名性を指摘する。どこまでも言語化を拒む無分節の「何か」であって、だからこそ東洋は存在の極所に種々の名称すなわち、「無」「真」「道」「空」などなど便宜上の「仮名」（けみょう）をつけ、コトバ圏内にこれを引き入れた……。 と、こう追えば、「古代普遍の哲人の叡智」が、みな同じところに立っていることが見えてこよう（井筒はこれをイスラーム圏まで俯瞰して説いている）。 おそらく三善もまた、この叡智を直覚していた。セーヌの暗い川底と、信州の山肌を縫い昇る慕わしい母の煙の行方の間に。それが「遠方より無へ」の朧な眺めであった。 ゆえ、ここで立ち止まり、もう一度、青春期に馴染んだフランス実存主義を別の方向から検証、あるいは自己点検しよう、とフッサールの現象学「ノエシス・ノエマ」に足を踏み入れたのだ。 ＊ ＊ ＊ カミュは、おそらく三善にとって最も近しい西欧だったのではないか。私は『レオス』の背後にもう一つ、『異邦人』(窪田啓作訳p.6)の最初の句が響くのを聴く。 「Aujourd’hui, maman est morte.」 きょう、ママンが死んだ。 そう、母が死んだ、のだ。 だが続く、 「Ou peut-être hier, je ne sais pas.」 もしかすると、昨日かも知れないが、私にはわからない。 もしかすると〜わからない、は、殺人を犯した理由を「太陽のせい」とする主人公ムルソーが、最終節でママンを思い出し、最後の「望み」として口にする終句「すべてが終わって、私がより孤独でないことを感じるために、この私に残された望みといっては、私の処刑の日に大勢の見物人が集まり、憎悪の叫びをあげて、私を迎えることだった。」（p.127）と響き合う。神への懺悔を促す司祭を憤怒とともに独房から叩き出したムルソーが最後に悟った「幸福」を、三善は覗き込む。 永遠の生死の瀬音は、何処へ自分を誘なおうとしているのか。 （続く） (2026/8/15) 参考資料) ◆書籍 『遠方より無へ』三善晃著 白水社 1979 『鬩ぎ合うもの超えゆくもの』丘山万里子著 深夜叢書社 1990 『波のあわいに』三善晃＋丘山万里子 春秋社 2006 『ブッダの言葉』中村元訳 ワイド版岩波文庫7 2007 『転落』カミュ 前山悠新訳 光文社 2023 『異邦人』カミュ items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于日本当代作曲家三善晃作品《レオス》（1976）的深度音乐评论，属于系列乐评的第13篇。文章从哲学与文学视角切入，详细追溯了三善从西欧存在主义（卡缪、加缪、萨特）经现象学到东方佛教思想的内在转向。评论者丘山万里子通过三善的《転落》引用、冬日阿姆斯特丹的记忆、以及对「死」与「无」的反复追问，揭示了《レオス》背后的精神轨迹——从实存苦的地狱圆环到「眺め」中水的静谧。文本深度结合哲学文本解读与作曲家的自述，分析了1970年代初三善在能乐、《レクイエム》中对实存主义的超越过程。乐评本身学术性强，但未直接对音乐本体（音响、织体、结构）作技术分析，更多是思想史式的解读。

items.body:
Hair-kissing house shuffle, ambient-breaks, and offbeat electro, from a regular of Nous'klaer Audio and Studio Barnhus, returning to Tokyo’s Mule Musiq.

Effortlessly poised for festival waft-offs, the ‘Ever Changing EP’ cycles thru the night from a kinked kind of cumbia house shuffle stroked with lush subs and layered with angel breath pads in ‘Through You’, to ambient breaks nodding to early AFX on ‘Unfold’, while tucking away a romantic, harmonised house slug in ‘Multitudes’, and snapping to dusted electro-breaks on the moodier closer, ‘Continuum’.
items._cn_summary: 这张EP由Nous'klaer Audio和Studio Barnhus的常客Martinou发行于东京Mule Musiq厂牌，四首作品横跨夜晚的不同氛围。从融合cumbia律动的house律动开场，天使般的pad音色叠加在浓郁低音之上；中段以早期AFX风格的ambient breaks展开探索；随后是一首带有和声处理的浪漫house段落；终曲则转向更具忧郁气质的碎拍electro。整体风格游走于舞曲质感与氛围电子之间，既有舞池能量也保留冥想空间，呈现出夜晚渐变的色彩流转。

items.body:
Chunky vocal house and kinkier depth by the German veterans of Innervisions, Kompakt, et al, doing it for Tokyo’s finest.

Disciples of Âme’s big chords and haughty NYC-style shunt will be all over the gospel house pomp of ‘Rock A Lott’, primed for the biggest rooms you can lay hands on, whilst ‘Take Me Back’ dials it down to a more purring, prowling deep house swang and parry threaded with blunted vox and Levon Vincent-Like chords.
items._genre: vocal house / deep house / gospel house
items._cn_summary: 这张作品由两位长期活跃于独立电子音乐场景的德国制作人合作，主打厚实人声与强劲律动。标题曲采用宏大的福音浩室和弦，结构直接，冲击力适合大空间播放；《带我回去》则收束为更低沉、潜行感更明显的深度浩室，以钝化人声切片和近似纽约地下俱乐部音乐的冷峻和弦推进。整体强调舞池功能性、成熟编曲与细节层次，声音虽未呈现明显的实验突破，但相较同质化的主流电子制作，仍保有内敛、锋利且辨识度较高的俱乐部气质。
